Environment and GPU setup

Verify your Python environment, choose a backend, and complete one tiny CPU simulation.

Install and fetch tables once

Use Python 3.13 or newer. Locally, create an environment and install: 
uv venv --python 3.13
uv pip install 'pyrite-mc[apps]==0.22.4'
uv run pyrite tables fetch
uv run pyrite tables verify
uv run marimo edit docs/notebooks/00-setup.py
The reference data download is about 100 MB. Fetch verifies archive SHA-256 before installation; tables verify checks installed pins and payloads. The setup cell calls _ = pyrite.fetch_tables() to install missing pinned tables automatically. Complete installations are reused without a network request. The CLI commands above remain useful for manual verification or troubleshooting. See the tables reference. Molab: open the badge above; its inline dependency manifest installs the CPU environment. The first cell fetches missing tables automatically; you can run pyrite tables verify in Molab's terminal. Start with CPU. If your Molab session offers an NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000, select that GPU in Molab, then install the NVIDIA extra into the same environment: 
uv pip install 'pyrite-mc[nvidia]==0.22.4'
nvidia-smi
Use the same extra for a local NVIDIA GPU. A compatible NVIDIA driver is still required; the current extra supplies CUDA 13 CuPy/toolkit packages. GPU type, availability and account quotas depend on the host. This notebook does not require a GPU or allocate GPU transport by default.

Choose the backend before import

The first code cell sets PYRITE_MC_BACKEND to cpu unless the environment already selected another backend. For GPU execution, set it to cuda before importing PyRITE. Restart the kernel after changing the backend or installing CuPy; rerunning a later cell does not undo imports cached in a live kernel. The smoke result below records the actual backend, which should match your selection. nvidia-smi confirms driver/GPU visibility; importing CuPy alone does not prove a compatible device exists.

Continue

This tiny, fixed-seed run verifies that the selected backend can produce finite, nonzero spectral data with the installed tables. It is not a convergence or physics-validation test. The histories are numerical samples, not a physical beam charge. Check the validation status for scientific evidence and limitations. Continue with 01 — Your first X-ray spectrum. Keep the core sequence on CPU until workload size justifies a GPU. GPU outputs can differ across architectures; compare physically meaningful quantities with justified tolerances, not exact random-history identity.
